subtype: Boss expects excellence or expects nothing [Receiver]
passage: Tanuja, you asked why I didn't apply for the full-time job. Okay. There were two of us interning at the design studio: Jai and me, Nikita, the resizing queen. On day one, the manager looked at Jai's portfolio and said, "You'll do great things here." She flipped through mine and said, "Good, we need help with resizing." And that was it, for three months. Jai got the client pitch, the late-night reviews, red pen all over his drafts. I got banners to resize. Nobody corrected my work, because nobody looked at it. By week six I stopped staying late. Why would I? Jai got better every week; I could see it. I think I could have too. But it's hard to rise when nobody hands you anything heavy to lift.

qa.q: What did the manager say to Jai on day one?
qa.a: "You'll do great things here."

qa.q: Why did Nikita stop staying late by week six?
qa.a: Nikita felt discouraged, since nobody expected much: there were no real tasks and nobody even looked at the work, so extra effort seemed pointless. 😔

qa.q: What could Nikita have tried around week six instead of giving up?
qa.a: Nikita could have asked the manager directly for one harder task and for feedback on the banners, testing whether the low expectation could change.

qa.q: How might the internship have looked from Jai's side?
qa.a: Jai was handed the pitch, the reviews and honest red-pen feedback, so the manager's belief became real chances to grow; Jai may not even have noticed how different Nikita's months were.

grounding: A young intern treated as filler gets no stretch tasks or feedback and coasts, while the intern the manager expected much from rises.

subtype: Boss expects excellence or expects nothing [Receiver]
passage: I'm Disha, a year into my job at the bank branch, and I watched this summer's two interns. On day one the branch manager told Mehak, "I've heard you're sharp. I'll expect a lot." He gave her the loan-file audit and sat with her every Friday to go through her mistakes, line by line. Sometimes she came out red-faced. By August she was catching errors I had missed. The other intern, Sameer, got the photocopier and the visitor register. The manager never asked his opinion and never checked his work. Sameer started arriving late and leaving early, and nobody noticed. I can't say what either of them felt. But on the last day, Mehak got an offer letter, and Sameer got a handshake.

qa.q: What did the manager give Mehak to work on?
qa.a: The loan-file audit.

qa.q: What might Mehak have been feeling when she came out of the Friday reviews red-faced?
qa.a: She may have felt embarrassed by her mistakes, yet the high expectation seemed to push her to improve, since by August she was catching errors others missed.

qa.q: What could the manager have done differently for Sameer?
qa.a: He could have given Sameer a real task and the same Friday feedback instead of only the photocopier, so Sameer had a chance to rise too.

qa.q: What might the summer have been like for Sameer?
qa.a: Sameer was never asked for an opinion or checked on, so he may have felt invisible, and coasting became easier than trying.

grounding: A young employee watches one intern who is expected to excel get real work and feedback and rise, while another treated as filler coasts.

subtype: Boss expects excellence or expects nothing [Receiver]
passage:
Week 1: Uma's first internship at the NGO office meant filing and tea orders. The coordinator barely learned her name. By Friday she was scrolling her phone at her desk by eleven.
Week 3: The coordinator left, and Jaya took over. She read Uma's college project on village water use and said, "This is good thinking. I want you on the survey report, and I'll give you honest notes." The notes came back covered in comments. Uma stayed late fixing every one.
Week 8: Uma presented the survey findings to the funders. Her voice shook for the first minute, then steadied. Afterwards she realised she hadn't looked at her phone all day.

qa.q: What was Uma doing at her desk by eleven in week 1?
qa.a: She was scrolling her phone.

qa.q: Why did Uma stay late fixing every comment in week 3?
qa.a: Jaya's belief that her thinking was good made the effort feel worthwhile, and she wanted to live up to it.

qa.q: What was the turning point, and what made it work?
qa.a: Jaya giving Uma a real report along with honest notes; the high expectation came with real work and feedback, not just praise. 🙂

qa.q: How might the funders see Uma in week 8 compared with how the old coordinator saw her?
qa.a: The funders see a capable intern presenting findings, while the old coordinator saw someone for filing and tea and never found out what she could do.

grounding: An intern treated as filler coasts, then rises once a new manager expects good work and gives her stretch tasks and honest feedback.

subtype: Manager checks own expectations [Response]
passage:
Dear Charu Ma'am,
You once told me to check my own patterns, so here is a confession. Last month I looked at the task tracker for my team of four. Every tricky client problem had gone to Ankit. Every routine data-cleaning job had gone to Farzana. I never decided that on purpose. It just felt natural, because Ankit "seemed quick" in his first week.
So I changed it. This month all four get one hard problem each, the same fifteen-minute feedback chat every Friday, and the same patience when they ask questions. I'm judging by what they deliver, not by my first impression.
Two weeks in, Farzana's fix for a billing issue was the best in the team. I nearly never found out.
Gratefully,
Rekha

qa.q: What kind of jobs had gone to Farzana?
qa.a: Every routine data-cleaning job.

qa.q: How did Rekha feel on finding that Farzana's fix was the best, and why?
qa.a: Rekha seems relieved and a little shaken ("I nearly never found out"), realising the old pattern would have hidden what Farzana could do.

qa.q: Which changes did Rekha make, and why are they fair?
qa.a: All four now get one hard problem, the same Friday feedback chat and the same patience, and are judged by what they deliver, so no first impression decides anyone's chances.

qa.q: How might Farzana have experienced the months before the change?
qa.a: Farzana kept getting routine jobs without knowing why, and may have felt stuck or overlooked, with no chance to show what Farzana could do.

grounding: A young manager notices hard tasks went to one person and routine ones to another, then gives everyone the same challenge, feedback and patience.

subtype: Manager checks own expectations [Response]
passage: Honestly? What surprised me most in my first year as kitchen manager was me. I'm Deepika, twenty-five, and I run the kitchen at a hotel in Kochi. For months I gave the new dishes to Suresh and the chopping to Farida. When a sauce went wrong, I'd explain it patiently to Suresh and just fix it myself for Farida. One night I watched her standing by the prep counter while Suresh plated my new fish curry, and I thought: when did I decide she couldn't? I had no evidence. So I made a rule. Everyone rotates through the new dishes, everyone gets the same tasting feedback, and I write down what actually happens. Farida's first attempt was average. Her third was the best version we've served.

qa.q: Where does Deepika run the kitchen?
qa.a: At a hotel in Kochi.

qa.q: What was Deepika thinking while watching Farida at the prep counter?
qa.a: Deepika wondered when the decision that Farida couldn't handle new dishes had been made, and realised there was no evidence for it. 🤔

qa.q: Which rule did Deepika make, and why does writing things down matter?
qa.a: Everyone rotates through new dishes with the same tasting feedback, and Deepika records results; writing down what happens means judging by evidence, not impressions.

qa.q: How might the kitchen feel different to Farida after the rotation?
qa.a: Farida finally gets new dishes and real feedback instead of only chopping, so the kitchen can become a place to grow, and her third attempt shows it.

grounding: A young kitchen manager notices a habit of giving new dishes to one cook and chopping to another, then gives everyone the same chances and judges by results.

subtype: Manager checks own expectations [Response]
passage: I'm Jasleen, and I've worked under Rajni at the call centre for a year. In her team meeting last Monday, she did something I've never seen a manager do. She put up the list of who had handled the escalation calls: nine to Varun, none to Gulnaz. Then she said, "I didn't plan that. I think I just expected more from Varun. That isn't fair." From that day, escalations rotate, and each of us gets the same ten minutes of feedback after a hard call. When Gulnaz fumbled her first escalation, Rajni didn't take it back; she listened to the recording with her and let her try again. I don't know what Gulnaz felt, but she asks questions in meetings now, which she never did before.

qa.q: How many escalation calls had gone to Gulnaz?
qa.a: None.

qa.q: Why do you think Rajni showed the list to the whole team?
qa.a: She seemed uncomfortable with an unfair pattern she hadn't planned, and wanted to fix it openly so everyone knew things would change.

qa.q: What choice did Rajni make when Gulnaz fumbled her first escalation, and why does it matter?
qa.a: She didn't take the calls back; she went through the recording with Gulnaz and let her try again, giving her the same patience others had got.

qa.q: How might Varun feel about the change?
qa.a: Varun loses some hard calls and the quiet special status, which might sting a little, though the same fair feedback now applies to Varun as well.

grounding: A colleague watches a young manager admit she gave hard calls to one person and none to another, then rotate them with equal feedback and patience.

subtype: Parent who is sure of what the child is [Actor]
passage: I'm Vishal, Rajni's neighbour on the third floor. Her son Bittu is four. Whenever anyone speaks to him in the lift, Rajni answers first: "He's the shy one, he won't talk." Yesterday the watchman asked Bittu his name. Bittu opened his mouth, and Rajni said, "Bittu. Sorry, he's very shy." Bittu closed his mouth and hid behind her dupatta. At the building's Holi party, she kept him on her lap instead of letting him join the water-balloon game, saying he'd hate it. Yet I've seen Bittu chatter to my dog through the balcony railing for ten minutes straight. I don't know what goes on in either of their heads. But I wonder if he's learning that his voice isn't needed.

qa.q: What did Bittu chatter to through the balcony railing?
qa.a: Vishal's dog.

qa.q: What does Rajni answering for Bittu suggest about how she sees him?
qa.a: She seems sure he's "the shy one" who won't talk, so she steps in before he gets a chance, perhaps to protect him.

qa.q: What could Rajni try the next time someone speaks to Bittu in the lift?
qa.a: She could wait quietly and give him time to answer himself, even slowly, showing she expects he can.

qa.q: How might being called "the shy one" feel to Bittu over time?
qa.a: He might start to believe his voice isn't needed and hide more, even though he clearly chatters away when nobody is labelling him.

grounding: A neighbour watches a young mother convinced her son is the shy one answer for him and keep him from chances, so he plays the role.

subtype: Parent who is sure of what the child is [Actor]
passage:
Monday: At the school gate, Kiran's teacher asked her about the weekend. Baljeet answered for her, as always. "She's the shy one, ma'am." Kiran, five, stared at her shoes.
Thursday: At her cousin's birthday party, the magician asked for a helper. Kiran's hand twitched upward. Baljeet caught it gently. "You won't like it, beta." She sat back and watched the other children laugh on stage.
Next Monday: Baljeet had spent the weekend thinking about that twitching hand. At the gate, when the teacher asked about the weekend, he said nothing. The silence felt long. Then Kiran whispered, "We went to the lake." Then, louder, "There was a duck with no tail!"

qa.q: What did Kiran say about the duck?
qa.a: There was a duck with no tail.

qa.q: Why did Baljeet keep thinking about Kiran's twitching hand over the weekend?
qa.a: He seemed to realise she had wanted to volunteer, and that his certainty that she was "the shy one" had held her back.

qa.q: What choice did Baljeet make the next Monday, and what did it show?
qa.a: He stayed silent and let Kiran answer herself; given room and time, she spoke, first in a whisper and then louder. 😊

qa.q: What might Thursday's party have felt like for Kiran?
qa.a: Her hand showed she wanted to go up, so being held back while other children laughed on stage may have felt disappointing and taught her again that she is the one who watches.

grounding: A young father sure his daughter is the shy one answers for her and holds her back, until he gives her room and she begins to speak.

subtype: Parent who is sure of what the child is [Actor]
passage: Anand, you keep telling people little Meenu is "the shy one." Your old father Tarun has made that mistake before, so listen. When I was twenty-five and your sister Sunita was three, I decided the same about her. At every wedding I answered for her: "Sunita doesn't dance, she's shy." When the school wanted her in the annual-day play, I said no before she could speak. And she became exactly what I said: quiet, always behind a pillar. Then your mother went to her village for a month, and I was alone with Sunita. With nobody speaking for her, she ordered at the sweet shop, argued with the milkman, sang in the bath. I had been building her a small room and calling it her nature. Today Sunita teaches a class of forty. Give Meenu some room.

qa.q: What did young Tarun say at weddings about Sunita?
qa.a: "Sunita doesn't dance, she's shy."

qa.q: What did Tarun realise during the month alone with Sunita?
qa.a: He realised that by answering for her he had been "building her a small room" and calling it her nature, since without him speaking for her she ordered, argued and sang.

qa.q: What choice is Tarun asking Anand to make now?
qa.a: To stop calling Meenu "the shy one" and give her room to speak and try things herself, instead of answering for her.

qa.q: How might Sunita have experienced being "the shy one" as a child?
qa.a: Her father kept speaking and refusing for her, so she may have felt there was no space to try, and quietly became the girl behind the pillar.

grounding: An elder recalls how, as a young father sure his daughter was shy, he answered for her and she adopted the role until she was given room.

subtype: Small treat seems big or small by comparison [Actor]
passage: At the day-care snack table, Sheela Ma'am handed out plain round biscuits. Gurleen, five, nibbled hers slowly. Then Sheela Ma'am opened a new tin. "Surprise! Chocolate cream ones today." Gurleen got one and squealed, bouncing on her chair. "Best day!" Next, her little brother Nilesh got his, a big round one with a jam heart in the middle. Gurleen's face crumpled. She looked at her small cream biscuit, then at his. Her eyes filled. "His is bigger," she whispered, pushing hers away. A minute ago it had been the best biscuit in the world.

qa.q: What was in the middle of Nilesh's biscuit?
qa.a: A jam heart.

qa.q: Why did Gurleen squeal "Best day!" at first?
qa.a: After the plain biscuit, the chocolate cream one seemed wonderful by comparison, so she felt thrilled.

qa.q: How could Sheela Ma'am help when Gurleen pushes her biscuit away?
qa.a: She could kneel beside her, name the feeling ("You wanted a big one too") and remind her how happy the cream biscuit made her a minute ago.

qa.q: What might it be like for Nilesh when his sister starts crying about his biscuit?
qa.a: Nilesh may feel confused, or a little guilty, holding a big biscuit that has suddenly made his sister sad.

grounding: A young girl is delighted with a cream biscuit after a plain one but tearful when her brother gets a bigger one; the comparison changes the feeling.

subtype: Small treat seems big or small by comparison [Actor]
passage: I'm Irfan, Pooja's big brother. On Sunday, Mummy gave Pooja a small plain rusk, and she ate it without a word. Then Mummy gave her a biscuit with pink icing, and Pooja danced around the kitchen, holding it up like a trophy. Then Mummy gave me a big coconut cookie from the bakery. Pooja stopped dancing. She looked at her pink biscuit, then at my cookie, and her lip wobbled. "It's tiny," she said, and started to cry. Two minutes before, it was the best thing ever. I don't know what changed in her head. The biscuit didn't change at all.

qa.q: What was on the biscuit Mummy gave Pooja?
qa.a: Pink icing.

qa.q: Why did Pooja's lip start to wobble when she saw Irfan's cookie?
qa.a: Next to his big coconut cookie, her pink biscuit suddenly seemed tiny, so she felt sad and left out. 🥺

qa.q: What could Mummy do next time to avoid the tears?
qa.a: She could hand out the treats at the same time, or give similar sizes, and talk with Pooja about how happy the pink biscuit made her.

qa.q: How does Irfan see what happened to his sister?
qa.a: Irfan notices that the biscuit stayed exactly the same and only her feeling changed, though Irfan can't tell what went on inside her head.

grounding: An older brother watches his little sister go from joy to tears over the same biscuit once she compares it with his bigger cookie.

subtype: Small treat seems big or small by comparison [Actor]
passage:
Tuesday: After school, Farhan's Nani gave him a plain biscuit, then, as a treat, a small jam biscuit. Farhan beamed and ate the jam one in tiny bites to make it last.
Wednesday: Nani gave Farhan the same small jam biscuit. But his big brother Naveen came home from a birthday party with a huge chocolate cookie. Farhan looked at his biscuit, then at the cookie, and burst into tears. "Mine's a baby one!"
Friday: Naveen was at football. Farhan got the small jam biscuit again, alone at the table. He hummed, swung his legs and licked the jam off first.

qa.q: Where was Naveen on Friday?
qa.a: At football.

qa.q: Why did the same jam biscuit make Farhan cry on Wednesday but hum on Friday?
qa.a: On Wednesday, next to Naveen's huge chocolate cookie, it looked like "a baby one" and he was upset; on Friday nothing bigger sat beside it, so he was happy with it as a treat again.

qa.q: How could Nani help Farhan on Wednesday?
qa.a: She could comfort him, say it's hard when someone else's treat looks bigger, and remind him how much he enjoyed that same jam biscuit the day before.

qa.q: What might Naveen feel when his little brother bursts into tears over the cookie?
qa.a: Naveen might feel awkward or a bit guilty after coming happily from a party, or be tempted to share just to stop the crying.

grounding: Over a few days, a small boy loves a jam biscuit on its own but cries over it when his brother has a bigger cookie.

subtype: Marks judged against friends [Actor]
passage: I'm Ayesha, and I sit behind Keerthana. When the science tests came back, she got 14 out of 20 and smiled. Then she turned and saw Chandni's paper: 20 out of 20, with a star. Keerthana's smile dropped. She folded her paper in half so no one could see and put her head on the desk. At break she didn't eat her idli. Then Ma'am said, "This was a hard test. The class average was only 9." Keerthana sat straight up and unfolded her paper. "Fourteen is five more than average!" she told me, grinning. I don't know exactly what she felt. But the paper said 14 the whole time.

qa.q: What was the class average?
qa.a: Only 9.

qa.q: Why did Keerthana fold her paper after seeing Chandni's mark?
qa.a: Next to Chandni's 20 with a star, her 14 suddenly felt bad, so she seemed embarrassed and didn't want anyone to see it.

qa.q: What could Keerthana ask herself next time before reacting to a friend's mark?
qa.a: She could ask what she understood and what she missed, judging her 14 by her own learning instead of by whoever sits nearby.

qa.q: How does Ayesha see Keerthana's change of mood?
qa.a: Ayesha notices the paper said 14 the whole time and only what Keerthana compared it with changed, though Ayesha can't be sure what Keerthana felt.

grounding: A classmate watches a girl feel miserable about a fair score beside a friend's top mark, then delighted on hearing the low class average.

subtype: Marks judged against friends [Actor]
passage:
Monday: Rashmi got 32 out of 50 in maths and felt fine. It was more than last time.
Tuesday: At lunch, Yash said he got 48. "Only two wrong!" Rashmi pushed her rice around. At home she told Amma she was "the worst at maths in the whole world" and wouldn't show her the paper.
Thursday: Sir wrote the class scores on the board, without names. Most were in the twenties. Rashmi counted. Hers was the fifth highest. She ran home, slapped the paper on the table and said, "Amma, I'm actually good!" Amma looked at the paper. It was the same 32 Rashmi had refused to show her on Tuesday.

qa.q: How many marks did Rashmi get in maths?
qa.a: 32 out of 50.

qa.q: What was Rashmi feeling on Tuesday when she called herself "the worst at maths"?
qa.a: She felt miserable and ashamed, because Yash's 48 made her own 32 look tiny.

qa.q: What could Amma say on Thursday to help Rashmi next time?
qa.a: She could point out gently that it's the same 32, and ask how it compares with Rashmi's own last test, so her feelings rest on her own progress, not only on others' marks.

qa.q: How might Yash feel if he knew his "Only two wrong!" upset Rashmi?
qa.a: Yash was just happy about his score and probably didn't mean to hurt anyone, so he might feel surprised or sorry. 😅

grounding: Across a week, a girl's feeling about the same maths score swings from content to miserable to delighted depending on whose marks she compares it with.

subtype: Marks judged against friends [Actor]
passage: Usha, sit here. You're sulking because your friend got more marks, na? Let me tell you about your Vishal Dadu at ten. In our village school near Gorakhpur, I got sixty in the half-yearly exam. I was so happy, running home to show my mother. On the way, my friend Bhola showed me his: ninety-five. Suddenly my sixty felt like a stone in my hand. I hid the paper under my mattress and didn't eat my dinner. Next day, Masterji announced that most of the class had got below forty. Forty! I pulled that paper out so fast. I was a king again. Same sixty, Usha. Only the thing I held it next to had changed.

qa.q: What did Bhola get in the exam?
qa.a: Ninety-five.

qa.q: Why did young Vishal hide the paper under his mattress?
qa.a: Next to Bhola's ninety-five, his sixty felt like a stone, so he felt ashamed and didn't want anyone to see it.

qa.q: What choice could young Vishal have made on the way home that might have saved his dinner?
qa.a: He could have held on to how pleased he was before Bhola showed his paper, or found out how the rest of the class did before deciding his sixty was bad.

qa.q: Why might Dadu be telling Usha this story now?
qa.a: Usha is sulking over a friend's higher marks, and Dadu wants to show, through his own boyhood, that the feeling depends on what the marks are compared with.

grounding: A grandfather recalls how, as a boy, the same exam score felt shameful beside a friend's mark and wonderful once he heard the class did worse.

subtype: Feeling plain after scrolling edited photos [Actor]
passage:
Darshan: can't come to cricket today
Madhav: why
Darshan: idk. spent an hour on the photo app and now I look like a potato
Madhav: ???
Darshan: everyone on there has perfect skin and sharp jawlines. I looked in the mirror after and my face just looked... wrong
Madhav: those are filtered. half of them use editing apps
Darshan: I know but it still got in my head
Madhav: come anyway. nobody at the ground looks like that
Darshan: fine
Darshan: ok you were right
Darshan: the keeper had a pimple on his nose, the captain's hair was a total mess, and I looked completely normal
Darshan: same face as this morning lol
Madhav: 👍

qa.q: How long did Darshan spend on the photo app?
qa.a: An hour.

qa.q: Why did Darshan's face look "wrong" in the mirror after scrolling?
qa.a: Darshan felt insecure after an hour of perfect, filtered skin and jawlines, measuring a real face against edited ones, so an ordinary face seemed worse.

qa.q: What choice turned Darshan's day around?
qa.a: Going to cricket anyway after Madhav's nudge; among real teammates with pimples and messy hair, Darshan looked completely normal.

qa.a: Madhav can see a friend about to skip cricket over edited photos and knows that being among real people will reset the comparison.

subtype: Feeling plain after scrolling edited photos [Actor]
passage: In the Kottayam bus-stand shed, the evening bus was late again, and Mahima scrolled. Face after face slid past: glowing skin, perfect brows, not a single bump. When the bus finally came, she caught her reflection in its dusty window and turned away, pulling her dupatta over the spots on her chin. At home she didn't join the family in front of the TV and stayed in her room. Next morning at school, her cousin Sharmila was laughing with a smear of ink on her cheek. The girls in her row had oily foreheads, sleepy eyes, frizzy plaits. Mahima looked around and felt, strangely, completely normal. Her chin hadn't changed overnight. Only the faces around her had.

qa.q: Where was Mahima when she scrolled through the photos?
qa.a: In the Kottayam bus-stand shed, waiting for the late evening bus.

qa.q: Why did Mahima pull her dupatta over her chin?
qa.a: After scrolling through polished faces without a single bump, she felt ashamed of the spots on her chin and wanted to hide them.

qa.q: What small choice could Mahima try at the bus stand next time?
qa.a: She could put the phone away and look at the real people waiting, or read something else, so polished images don't set her comparison.

qa.q: How might Sharmila, laughing with ink on her cheek, see Mahima that morning?
qa.a: To Sharmila, Mahima is probably just her usual cousin; Sharmila isn't comparing faces at all, which is part of why Mahima feels normal beside her.

grounding: A teenage girl feels plain after scrolling polished photos, then feels normal among real classmates the next day; only the comparison set changed.

subtype: Feeling plain after scrolling edited photos [Actor]
passage: On Saturday night in Osaka, Aiko lay on her futon scrolling through photos of models: smooth skin, huge eyes, every hair in place. After an hour, she opened her front camera and quickly shut it again. She felt like a blurry photo. She texted Yuki, "I can't come to the festival tomorrow. I look terrible." Yuki wrote back, "You look like you. Come." On Sunday, among her classmates at the shrine festival, sticky with candy, hair flattened by the heat, faces red from running, Aiko forgot to check her reflection at all. When she saw a photo Yuki had taken of them both laughing, she thought, I look normal. Nice, even.

qa.q: Where did Aiko and her classmates go on Sunday?
qa.a: To the shrine festival.

qa.q: What does Aiko shutting her front camera so quickly suggest she felt?
qa.a: After an hour of perfect model photos she felt plain and self-conscious, "like a blurry photo", and didn't want to look at her own face.

qa.q: What choice made the difference for Aiko on Sunday?
qa.a: She went to the festival despite her text; among real, sticky, red-faced classmates, she stopped checking her reflection and saw herself as normal. 🙂

qa.q: What might Yuki have been thinking when replying "You look like you. Come."?
qa.a: Yuki probably saw the text as a worry about looks and wanted to remind Aiko she is fine as she is, and that being together matters more.

grounding: A teenage girl feels plain after scrolling edited model photos, then feels normal among her classmates at a festival.

subtype: Bargain looks cheap next to a costly item [Observer]
passage: Looking back, it's funny how fast it happened. Akash needed a shirt for his cousin's engagement, so we went into the mall store together. The first thing he picked up was a leather jacket: eleven thousand rupees. He laughed and put it back. Right beside it hung a cotton shirt for two thousand four hundred. "Aparna, look, this one's cheap," he said, already heading to the trial room. This is Akash, whose monthly pocket money is four thousand. I didn't say anything then. I just noticed that if we had come in through the other door, past the three-hundred-rupee T-shirts, the same shirt would have looked like a crime. Later, over chai, I told him. He went quiet, then laughed. "Two thousand four hundred is not cheap, na?"

qa.q: How much was the leather jacket?
qa.a: Eleven thousand rupees.

qa.q: Why did Akash call the shirt "cheap"?
qa.a: He had just seen the eleven-thousand-rupee jacket, so the shirt beside it seemed small, even though it was more than half his monthly pocket money.

qa.q: What choice did Aparna make, and why was the timing wise?
qa.a: Aparna stayed quiet in the shop and raised it over chai, which let Akash laugh and see it for himself instead of feeling judged at the counter.

qa.q: How might the shirt have looked to Akash if they had come in past the three-hundred-rupee T-shirts?
qa.a: Next to cheap T-shirts, the same shirt would have seemed expensive, and he might never have headed to the trial room.

grounding: A shopper notices a friend call a costly shirt cheap right after seeing a pricier jacket, showing how judgment follows the last thing seen.

subtype: Bargain looks cheap next to a costly item [Observer]
passage:
Outing note, Saturday — Leela, residence supervisor
Took five first-years to the market street for festival shopping. Chetan wanted a kurta. At the first shop he tried on a silk sherwani priced at nine thousand, laughed and hung it back. The shopkeeper then showed a cotton kurta for two thousand. "That's so cheap after the sherwani," Chetan said, reaching for his wallet. On the bus he had told me his budget was one thousand. I asked him quietly, "If you'd seen this kurta first, what would you think of the price?" He paused. "Expensive, actually." He put the wallet away and bought an eight-hundred-rupee kurta two shops down. Next outing I'll suggest students write their budget on a slip before we start.

qa.q: What was Chetan's budget?
qa.a: One thousand.

qa.q: Why did the two-thousand-rupee kurta seem cheap to Chetan?
qa.a: He had just tried on a nine-thousand-rupee sherwani, so the kurta looked small beside it, even though it was double his budget.

qa.q: Which question did Leela ask, and why did it work?
qa.a: "If you'd seen this kurta first, what would you think of the price?" It made Chetan judge the price on its own instead of against the sherwani.

qa.q: How might the order of showing clothes look from the shopkeeper's side?
qa.a: For the shopkeeper, showing the costly sherwani first makes the next item look like a bargain and helps sales; Chetan was reacting to that order.

grounding: A young supervisor watches a student feel a kurta is cheap right after trying a costly sherwani, and helps him judge it on its own.

subtype: Bargain looks cheap next to a costly item [Observer]
passage:
Sunday
Went bag shopping with Ritu. At the first store, she picked up a designer handbag, eighteen thousand, gasped and put it down like it was hot. Then the salesman showed her a "simple one" for four thousand five hundred. "After that, this is nothing!" she said. Ritu, who was complaining on Friday that she can't pay her phone bill. I wanted to say something but didn't know how without sounding like her mother. So I said, "Let's see the stalls outside first, then decide." Outside, bags were five hundred. She looked at the photo of the four-thousand-five-hundred bag on her phone, then at the stall, and said, "Oh. It's actually expensive, isn't it?" She bought a seven-hundred one. Felt like a good friend today.
Kalyani

subtype: Choosing the reference point deliberately [Response]
passage: Karthik, sit. I'm Asif, and yes, I overthink flats. The broker first showed me a two-bedroom with a balcony at double my budget, then a one-bedroom that suddenly looked "so reasonable." I nearly signed. Then I remembered how that trick works. I asked myself three things: what is this flat worth by itself, is it better than my old room, and what do I actually need? I work from the office, I cook, I need light. The one-bedroom was cramped and dark. A third place, never shown next to the fancy one, had a big window and a gas line, and it was cheaper too. The other thing: I had been scrolling my college friends' new-home photos every night. I muted them. I'm not living their highlight reel.

qa.q: What did the third flat have?
qa.a: A big window and a gas line.

qa.q: What was happening in Asif's mind when the one-bedroom looked "so reasonable"?
qa.a: Asif was pulled by the contrast with the costly two-bedroom and felt eager to sign, before recognising how that comparison works.

qa.q: Which three questions helped Asif choose, and why do they work?
qa.a: What the flat is worth by itself, whether it beats the old room, and what Asif actually needs; they replace the broker's comparison with Asif's own reference points.

qa.q: What would change if Asif had kept scrolling the friends' new-home photos every night?
qa.a: Every flat might have been measured against their best pictures, making even a good place feel like a failure and the choice harder to trust.

grounding: A young adult judges a flat by its own worth, against their own past and needs, rather than the nearest example or friends' highlight photos.

subtype: Choosing the reference point deliberately [Response]
passage: I'm Charu, Lavanya's flatmate. Last month her school group was all promotions, engagements and beach holidays, and I watched her go quiet after every scroll. One night she put the phone down and started a list on the back of an electricity bill. Left column: "Me, two years ago." Right column: "Me, now." Salary: doubled. Anxiety: much better. Friends: fewer, closer. Cooking: can make biryani. She read it out to me, laughing. Then she added a third column, "What I want next," with only two things: "Learn to drive. Visit Nani in Shillong." She hasn't left the group. She just looks at it less, and when she does, she scrolls quickly and shrugs.

qa.q: What did Lavanya write the list on?
qa.a: The back of an electricity bill.

qa.a: She may have felt discouraged and left behind, measuring her life against her friends' promotions, engagements and holidays.

qa.q: How did the list change what Lavanya compared herself with?
qa.a: She compared herself with who she was two years ago and with what she wants next, instead of her school group's highlights, and saw real progress.

qa.q: How does Charu see the change in Lavanya?
qa.a: Charu notices Lavanya laughing while reading the list and later scrolling quickly and shrugging, though Charu can only watch from outside. 🙂

subtype: Choosing the reference point deliberately [Response]
passage:
Monday: Vaibhav got a job offer from a small firm in Indore: decent pay, a short commute, a boss who asked good questions. He was pleased, until Indu mentioned that their classmate had just joined a big company in Mumbai. By evening, the offer felt small.
Wednesday: He sat down with Indu and a notebook. "Forget the Mumbai job," she said. "What is this offer worth by itself?" He wrote: "Pay covers rent and savings. Home food. Parents close. I'd learn the whole system, not one small part." Then: "Better than my internship? Much."
Saturday: He accepted. He muted the classmate's office-tour posts for a while, not out of envy, just so the offer could stay the size it really was.

qa.q: Where was the job offer from?
qa.a: A small firm in Indore.

qa.q: Why did the offer feel small by Monday evening?
qa.a: Vaibhav had been pleased, but after hearing about the classmate's big Mumbai job he was measuring his offer against that instead of on its own.

qa.q: Which question from Indu changed the decision on Wednesday?
qa.a: "What is this offer worth by itself?" It made Vaibhav list the offer's own merits and compare it with his internship, not with someone else's job.

qa.q: How might Indu have felt watching the good offer shrink in Vaibhav's eyes?
qa.a: Indu may have felt a bit guilty for mentioning the classmate, and wanted to help him see the offer clearly again.

grounding: Over a week, a young man stops judging a job offer against a classmate's and asks what it is worth by itself and against his own past.

subtype: Combo choice pushed by a pointless third option [Actor]
passage:
Friday: At the multiplex counter, Arnab read the board. Small popcorn: ₹180. Medium popcorn: ₹240. Medium popcorn and cold drink combo: ₹250. "Only ten rupees more for a drink? That's a steal," he told his sister Kalyani, and bought the combo with his birthday money. He felt very clever.
Sunday: Telling Kalyani about the film, he admitted he'd poured half the drink away. He had only really wanted small popcorn.
Next Friday: At the same counter, Kalyani pointed at the board. "Who buys medium without the drink?" Arnab stared at it. Then he shrugged. "It's still a good deal," he said, and bought the combo again.

qa.q: How much was the medium popcorn and cold drink combo?
Why did Arnab feel "very clever" buying the combo?
qa.a: Next to medium popcorn alone at ₹240, the combo looked like a drink for just ten rupees, so the deal felt smart, even though he only wanted small popcorn.

qa.q: At the counter the next Friday, what choice could Arnab make after Kalyani's question?
qa.a: He could ignore the medium-alone option and ask what he actually wants, which on Sunday he admitted was small popcorn.

qa.q: What might Kalyani notice about the board that Arnab doesn't?
qa.a: Kalyani sees that hardly anyone would buy medium popcorn without the drink, so that option seems to be there only to make the combo look good. 🤔

grounding: A teenager keeps choosing a mid-size popcorn combo because a pointless third option makes it look like a bargain, and the choice still feels smart.

subtype: Combo choice pushed by a pointless third option [Actor]
passage: Hemant, you think you're the first one a menu has fooled? Listen to your Raghav Chacha. When I was fifteen, the old talkies in our town put up a new board. Small popcorn, two rupees. Medium popcorn, four rupees fifty. Medium popcorn with a cola, five rupees. I bought that combo every Sunday for a year and told all my friends I'd cracked the system. Fifty paise for a whole bottle! I felt like a businessman. Your Dadi would ask, "Raghav, why are you spending five rupees when you used to spend two?" I'd say, "Because it's the best deal, Ma!" Nobody ever bought the four-fifty one. I never once asked why it was there. So next time a menu makes you feel clever, ask who designed it.

qa.q: How much was the medium popcorn with a cola?
qa.a: Five rupees.

qa.q: How did young Raghav feel about buying the combo every Sunday?
qa.a: He felt like a businessman who had cracked the system, proud of getting a whole bottle for fifty paise more.

qa.q: What could young Raghav have asked himself when his mother asked about the five rupees?
qa.a: He could have asked why anyone would buy the four-fifty option, and whether he actually wanted more than the two-rupee popcorn.

qa.q: How might Raghav's mother have seen his Sunday spending?
qa.a: She noticed he now spent five rupees where he used to spend two, so to her the "best deal" looked like more money leaving his pocket every week.

grounding: An uncle recalls how, as a teenager, a pointless middle option made a popcorn combo look like a bargain and made him feel smart for buying it.

subtype: Combo choice pushed by a pointless third option [Actor]
passage: The interval was nearly over, the queue was long, and Manoj and Siddharth had three hundred rupees between them. They had planned to share one small popcorn. The board flashed: Small popcorn, ₹150. Medium popcorn alone, ₹250. Regular combo, medium popcorn and a drink, ₹260. "Medium alone is two-fifty? Then the combo is basically a free drink," Manoj said. The bell rang for the second half. No time to think. He handed over two-sixty, grabbed the tub and the drink and ran. In the dark, he whispered, "Best deal ever." Siddharth whispered back, "We've got forty left for the auto home." Manoj crunched popcorn and kept watching, still sure it had been the smart buy.

qa.a: Three hundred rupees.

grounding: Under time pressure, a teenager picks a mid-size combo because a poor third option makes it look like a bargain, and feels smart about it.

subtype: Subscription tiers steer the choice [Actor]
passage:
Tuesday: Leela was signing up for a music app's student plan. Basic: ₹59, ads between songs. Standard: ₹169, fewer ads, one device. Premium: ₹179, no ads, four devices, offline downloads. "Ten rupees more for all that? Obviously Premium," she told Seema, and tapped.
Friday: Seema asked how many devices she used. "Just my phone." Offline downloads? "Haven't tried." Leela shrugged. "Still, it's the best value."
Next Tuesday: Her bank message showed ₹179 gone. She had meant to spend around sixty a month on music. For a second she frowned at the Standard plan, the one she would never have picked. Then she put on a song and decided she had made a smart choice.

qa.q: How many devices did Leela use?
qa.a: Just her phone.

qa.q: Why did Premium feel like the obvious choice to Leela?
qa.a: She felt confident it was clear value, because next to Standard at ₹169, Premium seemed to give everything for only ten rupees more.

qa.q: What question could Leela have asked before tapping on Tuesday?
qa.a: Which features she actually needs, since one phone and a few ads were fine, and whether she would still pay ₹179 if only Basic and Premium were shown.

qa.a: Seema's questions show Leela uses none of the extras, so to Seema the "best value" may look like paying for things Leela doesn't need. 😅

grounding: A young woman picks the premium plan because a barely cheaper middle plan makes it look like obvious value, though she uses none of its extras.

subtype: Subscription tiers steer the choice [Actor]
passage: Ritu, before you sign that plan, listen to an old man's story. I'm Arnab, and when I was twenty-one, a gym opened near my college hostel. The board said: one month, eight hundred rupees; three months, two thousand three hundred; one year, two thousand five hundred. Three months for 2300, or a whole year for just 200 more? I felt like a genius. I paid for the year out of my scholarship money. I went eleven times. Nobody I knew ever took the three-month plan. It just sat there looking silly, making the yearly one look like a gift. And I never even considered the monthly option, which is what I actually needed. So before you choose, cover the middle option with your thumb and see how you feel.

qa.q: How many times did Arnab go to the gym?
qa.a: Eleven times.

qa.a: The three-month plan at 2300 made the yearly one at 2500 look like a gift, so he felt sure he was getting great value.

qa.q: What does Arnab suggest Ritu try before choosing, and why?
qa.a: Covering the middle option with a thumb; without the odd plan in view, it is easier to see what is really needed, like Arnab's monthly option.

qa.q: How might Ritu feel hearing this just before signing?
qa.a: Ritu might feel a little uneasy about the plan in hand, but also grateful for a simple test to try before paying.

grounding: An older man recalls how, at twenty-one, a pointless middle gym plan made the yearly plan look like obvious value and steered his choice.

subtype: Subscription tiers steer the choice [Actor]
passage: Asif's final-year project files were due to his guide by midnight, and his laptop was out of storage. On the sign-up page, a red timer ticked: "Offer ends in 09:54." Plan A: 50 GB, ₹75 a month. Plan B: 100 GB, ₹210. Plan C: 2 TB, ₹220, plus photo backup and family sharing. "Karthik, ten rupees more for twenty times the space!" he said. Karthik, eating chips on the bed, said, "You need about 20 GB." The Wi-Fi dropped, then came back. The timer said 03:10. Asif chose Plan C and felt a rush of relief, as if he had beaten the system. qa.a: About 20 GB.

qa.a: He felt relief and a sense of beating the system, because Plan B at ₹210 made Plan C at ₹220 look like a steal.

qa.q: With the timer running, what could Asif have done differently?
qa.a: He could have ignored the timer and Plan B, asked what he needed, about 20 GB, and picked Plan A, which covered his 18 GB upload.

qa.a: To Karthik, the only question is how much space the project needs; away from the timer and the odd middle plan, 20 GB is the whole story.
